bmt-2020-discrete-01.title: Fix the first element
bmt-2020-discrete-01.body:
The first element can be any of the $4$ symbols other than $B$, and the remaining $4$ symbols can be arranged in $4!=24$ ways: $4\cdot24=96$.

**Answer: 96**

bmt-2020-discrete-01.title: Complement
bmt-2020-discrete-01.body:
There are $5!=120$ permutations, and $4!=24$ of them start with $B$, so $120-24=96$ do not.

**Answer: 96**

bmt-2020-discrete-07.title: Factor and bound
bmt-2020-discrete-07.body:
Since $(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)=abc-(ab+bc+ca)+(a+b+c)-1$ and the equation says $abc-(ab+bc+ca)=a+b+c-1$, we get $(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)=2(a+b+c)-2$.

Put $r=a-1$, $s=b-1$, $t=c-1$, so $rst=2(r+s+t)+4$. If one of $r,s,t$ were $0$, the left side would be $0$ but the right side is positive, so $r,s,t\ge1$. Assume $r\le s\le t$.

- $rst=2(r+s+t)+4\ge10$ gives $t^3\ge10$, so $t\ge3$.
- $rst\le 6t+4$ gives $rs\le6+\tfrac4t\le7$, so $r^2\le7$ and $r\in\{1,2\}$.

If $r=1$: $st=2(s+t)+6$, i.e. $(s-2)(t-2)=10$, giving $(s,t)=(3,12)$ or $(4,7)$.
If $r=2$: $2st=2(s+t)+8$, i.e. $(s-1)(t-1)=5$, giving $(s,t)=(2,6)$.

So $(a,b,c)\in\{(2,4,13),(2,5,8),(3,3,7)\}$ up to order. The first two have $6$ orderings each and the last has $3$: $6+6+3=15$.

**Answer: 15**

bmt-2020-discrete-08.title: Lower bound on the size of a tree, then a construction
bmt-2020-discrete-08.body:
Everyone except Dexter lies in a binary tree headed by one of Dexter's recruits. Call such a tree "big" if it has at least $71$ people (a recruit whose downline has $\ge70$ people heads a tree of size $\ge71$).

**Claim.** A tree with $e$ executives and at least $71$ people has at least $72e+71$ people.

Induct on the size. If $e=0$ the claim reads size $\ge71$, true by assumption. Let $e\ge1$, and let the head be $H$.

- If $H$ is an executive, its two recruits head big trees with $e_1,e_2$ executives, $e=1+e_1+e_2$, and by induction the size is at least $1+(72e_1+71)+(72e_2+71)=72e+71$.
- If $H$ is not an executive, all $e$ executives lie in the subtrees of its recruits. A subtree with fewer than $71$ people has no executive (an executive heads at least $1+71+71$ people), so any subtree containing an executive is big. If two subtrees contain $e_1,e_2\ge1$ executives, the size is at least $1+(72e_1+71)+(72e_2+71)>72e+71$ by induction. If only one subtree contains executives, it contains all $e$ and has at least $72e+71$ people by induction, so the whole tree has at least $72e+72$.

**Bound.** Let $e$ be the total number of executives, found in $k\ge1$ big trees under Dexter (trees with executives are big). Summing, $72e+71k\le2019$ (everyone except Dexter), so $72e\le2019-71=1948$ and $e\le27$.

**Construction.** Take a complete binary tree on $27$ people (nodes $1,\dots,27$ with children $2i,2i+1$): it has $14$ leaves. Give each leaf two recruits, each heading a tree of $71$ people. Every one of the $27$ people is then an executive, and the total is $1+27+14\cdot2\cdot71=2016\le2020$ (Dexter, plus the tree); the remaining $4$ ambassadors can be recruited anywhere (for instance directly by Dexter) without affecting the $27$ executives.

**Answer: 27**

bmt-2020-discrete-09.title: Linear map on the torus
bmt-2020-discrete-09.body:
Since $\{ax\}=\{a\{x\}\}$ and $\{u+v\}=\{\{u\}+\{v\}\}$, three shuffles act on $p=(x,y)$ as the integer matrix $M^3$ taken mod $1$, where $M=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Computing, $M^2=\begin{pmatrix}10&5\\5&5\end{pmatrix}$ and $M^3=\begin{pmatrix}35&20\\20&15\end{pmatrix}$.

The point is fixed iff $(M^3-I)p\in\mathbb Z^2$, where $A=M^3-I=\begin{pmatrix}34&20\\20&14\end{pmatrix}$. The solutions $p$ in $[0,1)^2$ are exactly the points of the lattice $A^{-1}\mathbb Z^2$ in a fundamental domain of $\mathbb Z^2$; their number is the index $[A^{-1}\mathbb Z^2:\mathbb Z^2]=|\det A|=34\cdot14-20\cdot20=76$.

(A direct enumeration of the points $A^{-1}(i,j)$ lying in $[0,1)^2$ also gives $76$.)

**Answer: 76**

bmt-2020-discrete-10.title: Count squares modulo prime powers
bmt-2020-discrete-10.body:
By the Chinese remainder theorem $\psi$ is multiplicative over coprime moduli, so $\psi(3^i5^j)=\psi(3^i)\psi(5^j)$ and the double sum factors as $\left(\sum_{i=0}^4\psi(3^i)\right)\left(\sum_{j=0}^4\psi(5^j)\right)$.

For an odd prime power $p^\alpha$, $2$ is invertible, and $x^2+x\equiv r\iff(2x+1)^2\equiv4r+1$. As $x$ ranges over all residues so does $2x+1$, and as $r$ ranges over all residues so does $4r+1$. Hence $\psi(p^\alpha)$ is the number of squares modulo $p^\alpha$ (including $0$).

Count squares mod $p^\alpha$: besides $0$, a square has the form $p^mu$ with $m<\alpha$ even and $u$ a quadratic residue unit mod $p^{\alpha-m}$, which gives $\varphi(p^{\alpha-m})/2$ classes for each even $m<\alpha$. So the number of squares is $1+\sum_{m\text{ even},\,m<\alpha}\varphi(p^{\alpha-m})/2$.

- Modulo $3^\alpha$, $\alpha=0,\dots,4$: $1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 11,\ 31$, sum $49$.
- Modulo $5^\alpha$, $\alpha=0,\dots,4$: $1,\ 3,\ 11,\ 53,\ 261$, sum $329$.

The total is $49\cdot329=16121=7^3\cdot47$. The distinct prime factors are $7$ and $47$, with sum $54$.

**Answer: 54**
